title: Navigation
primary_metric: total drive time from the hotel to the hospital, in seconds, comparing driving at the posted speed limit (Option A, the Clean Run) against driving a stated amount over the limit on every segment (Option B, the Hot Run)

options.A: Stay at or under the speed limit for the entire drive (The Clean Run)
options.B: Speed to get Rachel to the hospital faster, risking Filberto's license and a $10,000+ fine (The Hot Run)

legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y3/Additional/Navigation/Case Study_ Navigation.docx + Guides Notes.docx) is preserved: the taxi-hail opening dialogue, Rachel and Thomas's situation (9 months pregnant, 2nd child, first labor 1.5 hours, labor started 20 minutes before the ride), Filberto (20-year Modus City taxi driver, just robbed of phone/cash), his known stop-sign/turn timing rules (4s stop, +2s left, +1s right, +1s straight), the road classification rules (divided highway = 45 mph no stop signs; every other road = 25 mph with a stop sign at every intersection), the near-zero-traffic Sunday-morning setting, Modus City's camera-enforced traffic law with permanent license loss and a fine 'over $10,000', and the Appendix A map (Portfolio13_Modus03.jpg, hotel/hospital pins) are all reused verbatim or near-verbatim from the source. The dilemma framing is locked per cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md (HIGH confidence -- 'already cleanly binary in the source'): A) stay at/under the limit the entire drive, B) speed to get Rachel to the hospital faster, risking Filberto's license and a $10,000+ fine. The source's Challenges section only vaguely asked for 'a drawing of the path' and 'the total time' without a computable route -- this conversion authors a concrete, internally-consistent four-segment route (Appendix C: Cannery Row, Fairview Ave, Route 9 highway, Harbor St; total 3.4 mi) consistent with the source's own map (one divided highway crossing the city, hotel and hospital pins on either side) and its own stated timing rules, since the source itself never fixed segment distances. The source also left 'how much faster' entirely to the student ('If you choose to speed... how much faster and on which parts of your path?') -- this conversion preserves that as the actual Challenge 3 deliverable (D3) and fixes +6 mph over the limit only as FACILITATOR.md's illustrative worked answer for the balance test, chosen specifically to keep the base-case margin under SPEC section 2's 20% cap (18.15%; +8 mph, the first value tried, produced 23.98% and was rejected as unbalanced -- see sensitivity_model.py history). D4 (the risk-in-dollars-per-minute-saved deliverable) and its Appendix D Modeling Assumption (one year of income as a conservative floor for a 'permanent' license loss) are new -- the source only stated the fine, never a computable total-risk figure. The Twist (Route 9 closed for construction, forcing an all-local detour) formalizes the original Guide Notes' one-line stub ('Twist: Construction closure') into a fully worked, internally consistent scenario with its own segment data (Appendix E of the guide, Fifth Ave + Ridge Rd) and its own recomputed margin (20.20%, breaking the 20% cap) -- this is new authorship consistent with the original guide's stated intent, not an invention of a new twist concept.

deliverables.text: A labeled route drawing from the Hotel to the Hospital, tracing the four segments in Appendix C over the map in Appendix A, with each segment's road name, distance, and speed-limit classification marked.

A segment-by-segment drive-time table for the Clean Run (Option A): distance divided by the posted limit converted to a time, plus every stop-sign delay, ending in one grand total elapsed time in minutes and seconds.

A second segment-by-segment drive-time table for the Hot Run (Option B), stating exactly how many mph over the posted limit was chosen for every segment, ending in its own grand total, plus the time saved versus Option A in minutes/seconds and as a percent.

A total-risk calculation: using Appendix D and Appendix E's sourced figures, compute the total dollar exposure of Option B if a single camera catches Filberto, then express it as a rate -- dollars of risk per minute actually saved -- plus the pitch's required original visual display of the data.

balance.argument_a: The real time gap between the Clean Run and the Hot Run is small -- 67 seconds, 18.15% of the Clean Run's own total -- because most of the route's delay comes from stop signs, not speed; the one highway segment (Route 9) is the only place speeding buys real time without a stop sign eating part of it back. Against that modest saving, Option B risks a fine north of $10,000 plus the loss of Filberto's only livelihood, conservatively priced at one year of the real U.S. median taxi-driver wage ($42,100, Appendix E S1) -- roughly $52,100 of total exposure -- on a route where zero traffic also means zero cover from the cameras.
balance.argument_b: Rachel's first labor ran about 1.5 hours start to finish and 20 minutes are already gone -- by that pace, something on the order of 70 minutes may remain, and second labors often move faster than first ones. 67 seconds is a small share of the whole trip, but it is not a small share of a shrinking safety buffer measured in minutes, and it is not a number Filberto gets back once it is gone. The fine is real and severe, but it is a number on paper; a birth going wrong in the back of a cab is not.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = total drive time (s), Hotel to Hospital, via sensitivity_model.py:evaluate(). Option A (Clean Run, posted limits): 436.6s (7:16.6). Option B (Hot Run, +6 mph over the limit on every segment, Appendix C/D): 369.5s (6:09.5). Margin = (436.6-369.5)/369.5 = 18.15%, B faster. D4's dollar-risk-per-minute figure ($52,100 total exposure / 1.12 minutes saved) is real, disclosed context supporting Argument A -- it is not the graded primary metric, matching the pattern used in cases/family-trip and cases/cardiology for a large, real, disclosed second axis that is not hidden but also not what margin_pct measures.

modeling_assumptions.text: D4's total-risk figure prices Filberto's permanent license loss at one year of the real U.S. median taxi-driver wage ($42,100, Appendix E S1) as a conservative floor, not an estimate of his full remaining career, since the case never states how many years of income a 'permanent' loss should count as. Appendix D.

sensitivity_note: The base-case margin (18.15%) is genuinely balanced and stated. It is NOT robust to a full +/-50% sweep of the case's own stated assumption dials (case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5; sensitivity_model.py FLEX list) -- at +50% on speeding_mph_over (6 -> 9 mph over), the margin rises to 26.9%, breaking the SPEC section 2 20% cap (no winner flip: B remains faster at every tested value, by construction). license_loss_years has zero effect on the graded primary metric (time) at either +/-50% -- it only scales the supplemental, non-graded D4 dollar-risk rate. Disclosed explicitly per Tier 2 probe 5's own requirement rather than left for a guide to discover live. See sensitivity_model.py and FACILITATOR.md's sensitivity-note section.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The case explicitly leaves 'how much faster' to the student (Challenge D3) -- FACILITATOR.md's +6 mph worked answer is one illustrative choice among many a Hero could legitimately pitch, not a fixed real-world measurement. A larger chosen speed increment is a real, defensible pitch a Hero might make; the case discloses that such a pitch produces a less-balanced case (margin above 20%) rather than treating +6 mph as the only correct answer.
